It's a lot of fun ... but only practical if you want to hunt in black powder season. Otherwise, it's just a hobby thing more or less. I have a couple of BP guns, both reproductions. One a Springfield Hawking Rifle .50 cal, the other a Pietta Navy Arms 1858 Remington revolver in .44 cal. I think it's fun just to load 'em up and shoot them from time to time. It's a lot of work though, but still a ball. To start, I think I'd try a single shot rifle of some kind ... you can go old school, or new school BP firearms, so that's another consideration. I prefer old school myself. I don't know what else to say that might be helpful for you, without a little more detail. But hey, give it a shot, I'm sure you'll enjoy.

This is my go-to BP forum:

https://www.thehighroad.org/index.php?forums/blackpowder.12/

It's fun. It's also cheap, and free of many of the annoying restrictions. Want a revolver mailed direct to your door? In most states, no problem. Want a short barreled shotgun? Sure, take two, they're small.

Pay attention to the safety stuff: There must be no air space between the powder and the ball. Don't let a hot ember in the bore turn your powder horn into a hand grenade. Use the right powder, and caps that fit.

Most petrolium-based lubes do not play nice with BP residue, they mix with it and form an asphalt-like substance that is very hard to clean off. Ballistol and water are good for cleaning, bore butter and similar products are good for lube. Mix vegetable oil and beeswax if you want to go old-school.

BP guns must be cleaned the same day they are shot. Everybody has their own tricks, just clean them well. A little shotgun choke lube on the nipple threads makes it easier to get them out again.

Every gun has it's own personality, and will exhibit the best accuracy with its own combination of projectile, powder charge, and cap.

If you get a brass-framed revolver, keep your powder charges light (15, maybe 20 grains max). Or get a steel-framed revolver and load it as stout as you want.
